metadata.title: Mind the gap: Uncovering student’s learning achievement disparities in Cambodian urban and rural secondary schools

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the 2022 PISA two-stage stratified sampling design (schools selected with probabilities proportional to eligible 15-year-old population size, then students sampled within schools). The authors explicitly address the clustered sampling structure by implementing cluster-adjusted standard errors (robust standard deviation calculations clustered by school) to obtain reliable inference for within-school correlated errors. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights (e.g., student design weights) or replicate-weight procedures, so the analysis should be treated as not clearly weight-adjusted for population representativeness. For replication with PISA microdata, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights and, if available, replicate weights to align with OECD/PISA variance estimation conventions, especially given the school-level clustering.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper models PISA mathematics and reading test scores as outcomes but does not describe how missing responses were handled (e.g., complete-case exclusion vs. imputation) or how missingness interacts with the estimation procedure. This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically include nontrivial missingness across background variables and test items, and the choice of missing-data strategy can affect distributional regression and decomposition results.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis extracts the Cambodia sample from PISA 2022 and uses PISA mathematics and reading scores as outcomes. The authors restrict the analytic sample to public secondary school students due to a small number of private school students (noted as 316, about 7% of the entire sample), which also prevents further stratification for quintile regression. Urban vs. rural school location is defined following Lounkaew (2013) using PISA 2009’s urban/rural definition (city/large city vs. village/small town/town). The UQR is estimated across the achievement distribution from the 10th to the 90th percentile, and standard errors are clustered/adjusted at the school level to reflect the two-stage sampling design.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Cambodia (public secondary students) — Mathematics achievement
main_findings.target_variable: Urban–rural achievement gap explained by tangible vs intangible factors (RIF-Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OBD decomposition: intangible (unexplained) share of the gap in mathematics is 61.3% at the 10th percentile, 63.5% at the 20th percentile, 50.3% at the 30th percentile, 44.0% at the 40th percentile, 28.0% at the 50th percentile, and declines to 21.8% at the 90th percentile (tangible vs intangible contributions reported across percentiles). Additional analysis (Mathematics achievement (UQR across percentiles; rural vs urban)): UQR coefficients by quintile (cluster-robust SEs clustered by school); no single predictive accuracy metric reported. Example effects: rural vs urban location is negative across all quintiles; school closure is negative across all quintiles except the 90th percentile. Observations: 1511 (urban) and 1942 (rural) for the UQR tables.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Cambodia data for mathematics achievement, the study leveraged student grade, waged labor engagement, household SES, COVID-19 school closure, and certified teacher share within a RIF-Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition framework to quantify tangible (explained) versus intangible (unexplained) contributions to the urban–rural gap, finding that intangible factors dominate the gap among low-achieving students (e.g., 61.3% at the 10th percentile) but their relative importance declines sharply at higher percentiles (down to 21.8% at the 90th percentile). This indicates that improving rural students’ outcomes likely requires strengthening intangible school governance and community/parental mechanisms that are not captured by measured resources, especially for the most disadvantaged learners.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Cambodia (public secondary students) — Reading achievement
main_findings.target_variable: Urban–rural achievement gap explained by tangible vs intangible factors (RIF-Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OBD decomposition: intangible (unexplained) share of the gap in reading is 73.1% at the 10th percentile, 53.2% at the 20th percentile, 44.0% at the 30th percentile, 46.0% at the 40th percentile, 29.3% at the 50th percentile, and declines to 42.6% at the 90th percentile (tangible vs intangible contributions reported across percentiles). Additional analysis (Reading achievement (UQR across percentiles; rural vs urban)): UQR coefficients by quintile (cluster-robust SEs clustered by school); no single predictive accuracy metric reported. Example effects: rural vs urban location is negative across quintiles; school closure is negative across all quintiles in both urban and rural groups except the 90th percentile. Observations: 1511 (urban) and 1942 (rural) for the UQR tables.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Cambodia data for reading achievement, the study leveraged student grade, waged labor engagement, household SES, COVID-19 school closure, and certified teacher share within a RIF-Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition framework to quantify tangible versus intangible contributions to the urban–rural gap, finding that intangible factors account for most of the disparity at the lower end of the distribution (73.1% at the 10th percentile) and that tangible factors become relatively more important around the middle percentiles (e.g., intangible drops to 29.3% at the 50th percentile). This indicates that rural reading improvement for low achievers may depend more on unmeasured mechanisms such as school management, autonomy, and parental participation than on measured material inputs alone.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses Cambodia’s PISA 2022 microdata (public secondary school students) and analyzes mathematics and reading achievement across the 10th–90th percentiles using unconditional quantile regression (UQR), with school-cluster adjusted standard errors to reflect PISA’s two-stage sampling. It then applies a Recentered Influence Function (RIF) Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition to quantify how much of the urban–rural achievement gap is attributable to tangible (explained) versus intangible (unexplained) components. The results show that rural schooling is associated with lower achievement across the distribution, with stronger disadvantages for low-performing students, and that student-related factors (e.g., gender, ECE, waged labor, SES, phone use) generally matter more than school-level variables. Decomposition results indicate intangible factors dominate the gap among low achievers (mathematics: 61.3% at the 10th percentile; reading: 73.1% at the 10th percentile) but decline toward higher percentiles. Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight usage and missing-data handling, and the fact that decomposition/unconditional quantile regression are not causal identification strategies.
